lessons.title: Care Personally, Challenge Directly
lessons.key_idea: Radical Candor means showing you care about someone as a whole person while also being willing to tell them clearly when their work falls short.

lessons.title: Four Ways Bosses Get It Wrong
lessons.key_idea: Most feedback failures fall into Ruinous Empathy, Obnoxious Aggression or Manipulative Insincerity, and Ruinous Empathy, staying nice to avoid discomfort, is the most common.

lessons.title: Ask for Criticism Before Giving It
lessons.key_idea: Bosses build trust by asking for feedback on their own work first and rewarding it when they get it, before they start giving criticism to others.

lessons.title: Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In Person
lessons.key_idea: Good guidance is humble, helpful, immediate and given face to face, with criticism usually in private and praise often in public.

lessons.title: Rock Stars and Superstars
lessons.key_idea: Every team needs both steady rock stars who want to master their role and fast-growing superstars who want new challenges, and a good boss learns which each person is.

lessons.title: Candor That Gets Things Done
lessons.key_idea: Candid relationships power a team's whole cycle of work, from listening, clarifying and debating to deciding, persuading, executing and learning.

plan.title: Radical Candor
plan.author: Kim Scott
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core framework, its main practical advice and several of its key anecdotes well, though I may not recall every minor detail.
plan.one_liner: The best bosses care deeply about people and still tell them the hard truth.
plan.summary: Kim Scott, who led teams at Google and Apple, argues that the best bosses do two things at once. They care personally about the people who work for them, and they challenge those people directly. Put those two dimensions on a grid and you get four ways of managing. Radical Candor sits where both are high. Ruinous Empathy is caring without challenging. Obnoxious Aggression is challenging without caring. Manipulative Insincerity is neither. Scott shows how to build candid relationships by asking for criticism before giving it, and by offering praise and criticism that is humble, helpful, immediate and in person. She also shows how to understand what motivates each person, whether they want rapid growth or steady excellence. She also lays out a practical process for getting things done as a team. The result is a guide to being a demanding boss without losing your humanity.
